items.title: Workplaces reduce AI 'tokenmaxxing' as rising costs prompt more disciplined AI usage and model routing strategies
items.originalTitle: AI 'tokenmaxxing' fades as workplaces look to cut tech spending
items.summary:
The corporate trend of maximizing AI token usage, known as 'tokenmaxxing,' is declining as companies face rising costs without proportional productivity gains. Initially celebrated in tech circles, heavy AI consumption is now seen as expensive and inefficient, leading to a shift toward more strategic and cost-effective AI deployment.

Executives from companies like Microsoft and Palantir have expressed concerns about the high expenses and data risks associated with excessive AI token use. Businesses are increasingly adopting AI model routing to assign tasks to appropriate AI systems based on complexity, aiming to optimize costs. Additionally, some firms are exploring open-source AI models from Chinese startups as lower-cost alternatives to leading U.S. AI products.

items.title: JetBrains tests 'Caveman' skill for AI agents, finds 8.5% token savings versus advertised 65%, with no quality loss on coding tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Does Speaking to Agents Like Cavemen Save 65% of Tokens? We Test
items.summary:
JetBrains evaluated the 'Caveman' skill designed to reduce token usage by making AI agents speak tersely, claiming up to 65% savings. Their tests on 82 paired coding tasks with forced activation showed only about 8.5% token reduction and roughly 10% cost savings, with no measurable degradation in task quality. The skill compresses narrative output but preserves code and tool calls, which dominate token usage in agent workflows.

The study highlighted that the advertised 65% savings apply mainly to chat-style Q&A, not to agentic coding tasks. Cost savings were sometimes offset by outlier tasks with high token counts. JetBrains recommends using the skill for style preference rather than expecting significant cost reductions in typical coding agent use cases.

items.title: Anthropic says some Claude AI users' shared chat logs were publicly accessible via search engines before being removed [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Some people's chats with Claude AI found to be publicly available online
items.summary: Hundreds of conversations with Anthropic's Claude AI chatbot, including some containing personal and work information, were found to be publicly accessible online through search engines like Google. The chats were available because users had chosen to share links, which were then indexed by search engines until the links were removed over the weekend. The launch positions GuardDuty alongside similar AI-assisted security investigation offerings from Microsoft and Google.

items.originalTitle: Cracking the code: can AI help us decipher ancient languages?
items.summary:
Researchers are applying AI to assist in deciphering ancient languages such as Linear A and Etruscan, which lack bilingual texts or known linguistic relatives. AI helps by rapidly testing hypotheses and identifying patterns across large corpora, tasks that would take humans much longer to perform. However, AI cannot independently determine meaning without an anchor like a known language family or bilingual inscription, limiting its ability to fully translate these languages.

A recent example involved an AI engineer using AI tools to support a hypothesis that Linear A is related to Semitic languages, assigning values to signs and compiling a lexicon. While AI accelerates pattern analysis and can restore damaged texts, verifying translations remains challenging due to the absence of native speakers or extensive reference materials. This underscores AI's potential as a research assistant rather than a standalone solution in ancient language decipherment.

The White House’s Office of the National Cyber Director circulated a draft of the framework to OpenAI, Anthropic and Google around two weeks ago, said the people, adding that the three companies jointly submitted their own edits. That’s according to several executives at cloud providers that purchase Nvidia AI servers. They told me that based on their initial tests, they expect the company’s upcoming Vera Rubin server racks to be much easier to install than Grace Blackwell racks were in 2025. Back then, Nvidia’s biggest customers struggled mightily with an array of new technologies they hadn’t dealt with before. Their struggles were kept quiet, at least until my colleagues reported on it. 

For cloud providers spending billions on hardware, every week spent troubleshooting new servers would delay bringing on lucrative compute capacity for AI customers. Setup delays could also stall orders and squeeze margins for data center builders.

items.originalTitle: Robotics Startup Tacta Shows Its Hand (and Glove)
items.summary:
As robotics companies explore new ways to collect the massive volumes of data needed to train the physical AI models that will power humanoid robots, one approach is gaining steam. Some robotics companies are relying on specialized gloves that people can wear while they carry out tasks at work or around the home. The gloves record information about wearers’ movements, providing data that robotics AI models can learn from.

One example is Tacta Systems, a three-year-old startup that has raised $75 million but kept a low profile so far. I recently toured Tacta’s Palo Alto headquarters for the first outsiders’ look at the gloves and robots it is developing.

“Why are we as humans really good at high value work?” asked Tacta co-founder and CEO Vikram Pavate. “We have amazing hands.”

Companies developing humanoid robots often emphasize the importance of anthropomorphic hands to allow robots to take on people’s jobs. Tacta agrees so much that it is leaving the rest of the humanoid body to other companies. Its three-fingered hand is perched on the end of an off-the-shelf industrial robot arm, which is mounted on a rolling base.
